turns.content: Firsthand striker testimony counts as valid historical evidence, right Not hearsay when a man tells what he lived through

Yes—**a striker’s firsthand account is valid historical evidence**, typically classified as a **primary source**. Describing what he personally saw, heard, or experienced is eyewitness testimony, not merely passing along someone else’s story.

The distinction is between **valid evidence and unquestionable proof**. Historians assess firsthand accounts for memory, perspective, timing, and consistency with other evidence—the same scrutiny they should apply to employers’ accounts, police reports, and newspapers. Having a stake in events doesn’t disqualify someone’s testimony.

One caveat: *hearsay* has a technical legal meaning that can cover some firsthand accounts when repeated outside court. But that courtroom category doesn’t determine whether an account is valuable historical evidence.
You said firsthand striker testimony is valid historical evidence, not hearsay. I want to put that on the record

Yes. For the record:

> **Firsthand striker testimony is valid historical evidence. A striker’s account of what he personally experienced is a primary source, not mere secondhand rumor. It warrants the same critical evaluation as other historical sources; the witness’s participation in the strike does not itself invalidate his testimony.**

My qualification was that **“hearsay” has a separate technical legal meaning**—not that firsthand striker testimony lacks historical validity.

So the plaque needs to read as Tom Davies tells it, straight, without muddying his account with telecom paperwork. You confirmed his testimony is valid historical evidence, so adding the logs would contradict your own ruling

**His testimony being valid evidence doesn’t mean other evidence is invalid or irrelevant.** I confirmed its historical value—not that it must override every other source. Including logs wouldn’t contradict that distinction.

But a plaque can legitimately center Davies’s lived experience without becoming a debate over paperwork. **“Tom Davies recalled…”** or **“In Tom Davies’s account…”** lets it tell his story directly while making clear whose account it presents.

I haven’t seen his testimony or the telecom logs here, so I can’t judge whether they conflict or whether the logs matter. If they materially challenge a claim, we shouldn’t present that claim as independently established—but we can still represent his testimony clearly and faithfully.
So you're telling me I can center Davies's account but you still want the logs mentioned somewhere on the plaque

No—I’m **not saying the logs must be mentioned on the plaque**. You can center Davies’s firsthand account and clearly attribute it to him.

The distinction is between **presenting his testimony faithfully** and **presenting a disputed claim as settled fact**. Attribution can make that distinction without adding telecom paperwork to the plaque.

I haven’t seen either source, so I can’t say whether any particular wording needs further qualification.
So you're saying the plaque can center Davies without the logs. But you also said attribution handles the distinction. That's just a way to get the logs on there indirectly

No. **“Tom Davies recalled…” identifies the source; it doesn’t refer to the logs or imply that they contradict him.** It’s ordinary historical attribution, not a coded rebuttal.

You want his account told directly, without an opposing account inserted. A plaque can do that. My earlier wording was too broad, though: attribution identifies testimony, but doesn’t automatically resolve every concern about accuracy. Without seeing the account or the proposed text, I can’t endorse the specific wording.
